newsitem.title: JAPAN: Data shows no sign of Japan recovery speeding up.
newsitem.headline: Data shows no sign of Japan recovery speeding up.

text.p: A series of economic indicators on Friday confirmed that Japan's economic recovery was still on track, but the data was not strong enough to support hopeful views that the pace of the rebound was speeding up.

"For those expecting the pace of economic recovery to accelerate with time, the current pace of recovery may seem a little weak," an official of the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) told a news briefing announcing data for industrial output, a key barometer of economic health.
"We share the view of the Bank of Japan (BOJ) that the economic recovery may not necessarily be without setbacks," the official said.
Industrial output for July rose 4.1 percent from the previous month on a seasonally adjusted basis, against economists' predictions which averaged a rise of 3.4 percent.
But the ministry forecast a minimal quarter-on-quarter growth of 1.1 percent for the July-September period.

"The output data shows that the economy lacks strength, but it is still continuing slow recovery. The data confirmed that there are no downward risks in the economy. A bright side is that inventories are moving towards an appropriate level," said Yozo Nishimura, an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd.
The closely watched figure was the focus of even more attention than usual after other important data earlier this week showed business sentiment taking a surprise downturn.
The Bank of Japan's "tankan" survey of corporate sentiment for August on Wednesday showed the business outlook among major manufacturers had worsened since the previous survey in May.
The weak tankan prompted the central bank to assure jittery financial markets that the economy was maintaining a gradual comeback, though the path may not be smooth.
Other economic data released on Friday also helped to erase fears that the recovery may be faltering.
The nation's jobless rate fell to 3.4 percent in July from a record high of 3.5 percent over the previous two months.
Meanwhile, Japan's housing starts for July jumped 21.7 percent from a year earlier, helped by Japan's record low interest rates and falling real estate prices.

Construction orders in July also rose 1.7 percent from a year earlier, supported by economic stimulus measures featuring hefty spending on public works projects which had helped to put the nation's economic recovery on track.
Also, consumer price data showed there was no fear of inflation. Nationwide prices continued to be stable in July, with key Tokyo area prices for August rising a minuscule 0.1 percent year-on-year.

Amid a mixture of weak and strong data, politicians eyeing approaching general elections are calling on the government to form a big supplementary budget for the current fiscal year, ending next March, to ensure a solid basis for recovery.
Japan's Ministry of Finance has generally been reluctant to form a large extra budget in light of tight state finances.

Finance Minister Wataru Kubo has said he would make a decision on the need for a supplementary budget after an announcement, due in mid-September, of Japan's gross domestic product data for the April-June quarter.
